title: Coherent feed-forward quantum neural network
abstract_summary: The paper introduces the coherent feed-forward quantum neural network (CFFQNN), a fully coherent, circuit-based QNN that mirrors classical feed-forward architectures by encoding weighted feature sums as rotation angles and using controlled rotations for inter-layer connections. The approach reduces circuit depth and CNOT gate counts by over 50% relative to common QNN models, keeps qubit count independent of the number of input features, and demonstrates improved classification accuracy on benchmark datasets (e.g., ~91% on Wisconsin breast cancer and ~85% on credit card fraud detection).
methodology_description: The authors propose a coherent feed-forward quantum neural network (CFFQNN) and a reduced-parameter variant (FixedCFFQNN). They simulate hybrid quantum-classical training pipelines using Qiskit’s Statevector simulator. Classical datasets (credit card fraud detection and Wisconsin breast cancer diagnostic) are preprocessed via PCA to reduce 30 original features to 7 principal components; the credit-card dataset is further balanced by undersampling. For each experiment they set a maximum qubit budget of seven, encode multiple classical features onto a smaller number of qubits for CFFQNN using sequential Ry rotations whose angles implement weighted sums z = Σi Wi Xi + b, then implement feed-forward layers by applying parametrized controlled-Ry gates (C Ry) between qubits to mimic perceptron connections (weights θij). The final qubit’s expectation value ⟨Z_N⟩ is measured and post-processed with a classical threshold/activation to produce binary labels. Training is performed by updating quantum circuit parameters with the COBYLA classical optimizer (iteratively until convergence; in one case 100 iterations are stated). Baselines comprise a standard variational QNN that uses the ZZFeatureMap for encoding and a RealAmplitudes variational ansatz, plus a classical MLPClassifier. Performance is assessed with standard classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) and resource metrics (circuit depth, number of CNOTs, number of trainable parameters, runtime).
experimental_setup: Simulations run with Qiskit Statevector simulator (noise-free), on a personal computer. Maximum qubit budget set to seven. Datasets preprocessed via PCA to 7 features; credit-card dataset balanced by undersampling. CFFQNN experiments encoded 7 features into 3 qubits (first layer), used a second hidden layer of 2 qubits, and a single output qubit (total six qubits) in reported examples.
dataset_used: Credit card fraud detection (originally 30 features; reduced to 7 via PCA; balanced by undersampling) and Wisconsin breast cancer diagnostic (originally 30 features; reduced to 7 via PCA). Both datasets sourced from Kaggle.

Preprocessing (PCA to 7 components, undersampling of majority class for credit-card data), hyperparameters (max qubits = 7), and optimizer (COBYLA) are described, but exact circuit parameter initializations and full repository link were not provided in the manuscript; reproduction should be feasible if the referenced GitHub code is obtained.
key_findings: [supported] The authors introduce the Coherent Feed-Forward Quantum Neural Network (CFFQNN), a circuit design that mirrors classical feed-forward neural networks and avoids intermediate measurements (i.e., is coherent) and demonstrate it in simulation.
[supported] In simulation on benchmark datasets, CFFQNN and a FixedCFFQNN variant outperform a baseline QNN using a ZZFeatureMap + RealAmplitudes variational circuit on classification tasks.

[supported] Reported empirical performance (simulator) improvements: CFFQNN attains ~91% accuracy on the Wisconsin breast cancer diagnostic dataset and ~85% accuracy on the (balanced, PCA-reduced) credit card fraud detection dataset, exceeding the compared QNN results by ~5–10% in the experiments.

[supported] CFFQNN requires substantially fewer quantum resources (circuit depth and number of CNOT gates) in the reported experiments—roughly a ~50% reduction in both depth and CNOT count versus the compared QNN configurations.

[supported] The FixedCFFQNN variant (initial-layer weights fixed/untrained) reduces the number of trainable parameters, speeds training, and still outperforms the compared QNNs in the reported simulations.

[supported] Additional simulated experiments (appendix) show CFFQNN improvements on other tasks: heart disease classification (CFFQNN 78.8% vs QNN 65.76%) and a regression task (student performance) where FixedCFFQNN achieved a much lower MSE (0.0102) than the compared QNN (0.1982).

[supported] The paper presents a data-encoding strategy that writes multiple classical features onto a small number of qubits via sequential Ry rotations on a qubit, reducing the number of feature-encoding gates in the implemented circuits (demonstrated in simulations).

[speculative] The claim that the CFFQNN’s qubit count is independent of the number of input features (i.e., it need not scale with feature dimension) is presented as an architectural advantage but is not fully empirically validated across large feature dimensionalities on hardware; in the paper this is argued theoretically and validated on small PCA-reduced datasets.

[speculative] Statements that the design makes CFFQNN especially suitable for near-term NISQ hardware and that it paves the way for practical, scalable QNN applications in real-world ML are forward-looking and not demonstrated on physical quantum devices in this work.

[speculative] The suggestion that replacing classical activation functions with controlled rotations and keeping all branches coherent provides practical advantages beyond the observed simulated benchmarks is conceptual and not established as a general, provable advantage.
results_summary: The paper introduces the Coherent Feed-Forward Quantum Neural Network (CFFQNN), a circuit-level quantum analogue of classical feed-forward networks that omits intermediate measurements and encodes multiple classical features per qubit via sequential Ry rotations. In statevector simulations (Qiskit) on PCA-reduced benchmark datasets, CFFQNN and its FixedCFFQNN variant outperform a baseline QNN built from a ZZFeatureMap + RealAmplitudes ansatz: reported accuracies are ~91% (breast cancer) and ~85% (credit card fraud), with additional gains on a heart-disease dataset and regression tasks. The authors also report roughly ~50% reductions in circuit depth and CNOT counts versus the baseline QNNs in their experiments, and show that the FixedCFFQNN can reduce trainable parameters while maintaining accuracy. Broader claims about feature-scaling independence and NISQ suitability are argued theoretically but remain speculative pending larger-scale validation or hardware demonstrations.
performance_claims: CFFQNN accuracy on Wisconsin breast cancer diagnostic dataset: 91% (reported in abstract).
CFFQNN accuracy on credit card fraud detection dataset: 85% (reported in abstract).
CFFQNN outperforms existing QNN methods by 5–10% on the reported classification benchmarks (abstract claim, supported by presented simulation comparisons).

CFFQNN achieves >50% reduction in circuit depth and >50% reduction in number of CNOT gates compared to the compared QNN implementations (reported in abstract and shown in resource-comparison figures).
Heart disease dataset (appendix): existing QNN accuracy 65.76% vs CFFQNN 78.80% (layer structure [2,3,1]); simpler CFFQNN [1,1,1] gave 76.09% (appendix).
Heart disease circuit complexity (appendix): baseline QNN depth 39 and 36 CNOTs; CFFQNN [2,3,1] depth 26 and 18 CNOTs; CFFQNN [1,1,1] depth 14 and 4 CNOTs.
Student performance regression (appendix): MSE for CFFQNN = 0.1869, FixedCFFQNN = 0.0102, existing QNN = 0.1982.

In the credit-card and breast-cancer experiments the CFFQNN architectures used 6 qubits encoding 7 PCA features into three first-layer qubits, with specific inter-layer controlled-Ry counts given (e.g., 16 controlled operations in the described credit-card setup).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors present simulation evidence that their CFFQNN achieves better classification accuracy and lower circuit depth/CNOT counts than a particular baseline QNN (ZZFeatureMap + RealAmplitudes) in the tested benchmarks. However, no demonstration of a provable quantum computational or general empirical advantage on hardware is provided; claims about scalability, independence of qubit count from feature dimensionality, and suitability for NISQ devices remain theoretical/speculative and are not validated at larger scale or on physical quantum hardware.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — The proposed CFFQNN architecture reports higher classification accuracy than a standard variational QNN on small benchmark datasets (≈91% breast cancer, ≈85% credit-card fraud) while using substantially fewer CNOTs and shallower circuits (claimed >50% reduction).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Training is hybrid: circuit parameters (weights, controlled-Ry angles) are optimized with a classical optimizer (COBYLA) in a classical-quantum loop, demonstrating a practical hybrid pipeline for QNNs.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Design choices (encoding multiple features into few qubits via sequential Ry rotations, controlled-Ry feed-forward layers) explicitly target NISQ constraints by capping qubit usage (max 7 qubits in experiments) and reducing entangling-gate counts.

#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments are run on a noise-free Qiskit Statevector simulator (no shots), so reported accuracy and resource metrics do not account for sampling noise or device noise.

#limitation:qubit-count — Empirical validation is limited to a maximum of seven qubits with PCA reducing original feature dimensions to 7; real-world high-dimensional financial data scaling is not demonstrated.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — No runs on real QPUs are reported; claims about NISQ suitability and gate-count reductions are not validated on hardware.
#limitation:noise — Impact of hardware noise or error mitigation strategies is not evaluated, leaving open whether resource reductions translate to real-device performance gains.

#limitation:data-encoding — The claimed independence of qubit count from input feature count relies on sequential encoding (summing features into rotation angles) and PCA pre-processing; this shifts complexity into depth/parameterisation and classical pre-processing, which may limit scalability or alter information content.
contradictions: #contradiction:scalability — The paper asserts qubit-count independence and NISQ applicability, but demonstrates results only on small, PCA-compressed datasets (max 7 qubits) in noise-free simulation; thus the claimed scalability to realistic, high-dimensional, imbalanced financial problems and noisy hardware is not substantiated by the experiments.
